extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent drafters, patent attorneys/agents, and startups preparing patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting patent claims that maximize enforceability and validity: emphasize novelty and advantages, write clear unambiguous language, balance breadth and specificity, and structure claims to provide fallback coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Unique Advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting claims, focus on the unique advantages and benefits of your invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlighting these aspects can help demonstrate the invention's novelty and non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Clear, Simple Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid technical jargon or complex sentence structures that might confuse the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each element of the claim should be clearly defined and easy to understand. If your invention involves specialized terminology, define these terms clearly within the claim or in the detailed description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Positive Language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using negative limitations or exclusions unless absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive language is clearer and less likely to cause confusion. Instead of saying what your invention does not include, specify what it does include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Breadth with Specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should cover a wide range of potential infringements but not be so broad that they lose enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to cover as many potential infringing variations as reasonable while ensuring the claim remains supported, novel, and non-obvious — overly broad claims risk invalidation or rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Limiting Language ("Patent Profanity")
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use words that unnecessarily limit the scope of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common 'patent profanity' to avoid includes: "necessary", "essential", "key", "every", "must", "never", "only", "absolutely", "critical", "important", "preferred" — these can be interpreted as limiting and shrink claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequately consider existing patents and publications when drafting claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to consider prior art can lead to claims that are not novel or are obvious. Such oversight might invalidate your patent or severely limit its scope; use prior-art searching to shape claim scope and distinguishing features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Be consistent in terminology throughout the patent document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using different terms to refer to the same component or feature can cause confusion and ambiguity; keep term usage uniform between claims, specification, and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a Layered Claim Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft independent and dependent claims in a hierarchical (layered) structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims provide variations and inherit all limitations of the claims they depend on. If the broadest independent claim is invalidated, narrower dependent claims can still provide protection — use dependent claims to capture fallback positions and preferred embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get Professional Review
rubrics_metrics.description: Have your claims reviewed by peers and patent professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fresh eyes (peers, patent attorneys/agents) can catch inconsistencies, ambiguities, and potential weaknesses that the drafter might have missed; professional review improves claim clarity, enforceability, and prosecution prospects.
